blocks.text: 2.4.2 Reading an LP Solver Log

GridCap's weekly funding LP (lesson 2.4.1) is moving into a scheduled job. Most weeks nobody looks at it. The week a planner says "the numbers look wrong" or "the run took an hour", the first thing anyone asks for is the solver's **log**: the lines a solver writes while it works, saying what model it received, what it removed, how each iteration went and how it ended. This lesson reads one log from top to bottom, then two logs of runs that went wrong, then the same facts in GLOP's and PDLP's words. GridCap is a fictional utility; its numbers are teaching data.
The Model
The log below is the log of the funding LP of lesson 2.4.1, unchanged. Stated in full, so the log can be checked against it line by line:
**Sets.** $`P`$ the candidate projects; $`Y`$ the plan's years, the first being $`y_0`$; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects.

**Parameters.** $`c_{i,y}`$, what project $`i`$ spends in year $`y`$ if it starts at its earliest start ($k, 0 in a year it is not worked); $`v_i`$, its NPV at its earliest start ($k); $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k).
**Variables.** $`0 \le f_i \le 1`$ for every $`i \in P`$, the share of project $`i`$ funded; $`r_y \ge 0`$ for every $`y \in Y`$, the money carried out of year $`y`$, with $`r_{y_0 - 1} = 0`$.
**Objective and constraints.**
On the medium portfolio, counted from the model the program built:
cash rows 10, must rows 39; share variables 400, carry variables 10
Ask for the Log With msg_cb, and Keep It as Lines

A solver writes nothing unless asked. MathOpt's `solve` takes a `msg_cb` argument, a function it calls with each batch of new log lines. Passing a list's `extend` method collects the whole log, in order, as a Python list:

def solve_with_log(model: mathopt.Model, solver: mathopt.SolverType,
                   params: mathopt.SolveParameters | None = None) -> tuple[mathopt.SolveResult, list[str]]:
    """Solve, and keep every log line the solver wrote, in order, in a Python list."""
    lines: list[str] = []
    result = mathopt.solve(model, solver, params=params, msg_cb=lines.extend)
    return result, [mask_times(line) for line in lines]

A list is better than the terminal: a scheduled job can write it to a file next to the result, and a test can search it. `mask_times` replaces every wall-clock time in the log with `<t>`, because times change on every run and this page quotes the log exactly as the program printed it. Nothing else in the log is changed. Every log below is the medium funding LP solved with `solve_with_log`.
The Header Says What the Solver Received
HiGHS, the course's default solver, starts by describing the model it was handed:

LP funding-lp has 49 rows; 410 cols; 706 nonzeros
Coefficient ranges:
  Matrix  [1e+00, 6e+03]
  Cost    [1e+01, 6e+03]
  Bound   [1e+00, 1e+00]
  RHS     [1e+00, 4e+04]

Check the first line against the model before reading further: 49 rows are the 10 cash rows and 39 must rows, 410 columns (variables) are 400 shares and 10 carries. A count that does not match what you meant to build is a bug found before any solving, such as a loop that added each row twice. The 706 **nonzeros** are the entries of the constraint matrix that are not zero: each cash row holds the spend of every project worked that year, plus its carry terms.
The four ranges give the smallest and largest absolute value of each kind of number, rounded to a power of ten:

rows: 1 (a carry, a must row) to 5,990 (a project's spend)

blocks.text: Ranges spanning a few powers of ten, as here, are normal. A matrix range like `[1e-04, 1e+07]` is a warning: solvers compare numbers against tolerances near $`10^{-6}`$ to $`10^{-9}`$, and coefficients eleven orders of magnitude apart make those comparisons unreliable. The usual fix is to change units (money in $M rather than $, for instance) before building the model.
Presolve Shrinks the Model Before Any Iteration

**Presolve** is a pass that simplifies the model before the algorithm starts: it fixes variables whose value is forced, removes rows that say nothing new, and merges what can be merged. Section 3 covers it for integer models (lesson 3.3.2). In the log:

Presolving model
10 rows, 370 cols, 603 nonzeros  <t>s
10 rows, 368 cols, 601 nonzeros  <t>s
Presolve reductions: rows 10(-39); columns 368(-42); nonzeros 601(-105)
Solving the presolved LP

Each line is the model's size after one round. `rows 10(-39)` reads "10 rows left, 39 removed": the 39 must rows, since $`f_i = 1`$ fixes a variable, and a fixed variable is a number, not a decision. 39 of the 42 removed columns are those fixed shares; the other 3 went in further reductions (GLOP's log at the end of this lesson names its own steps). What remains is the real problem: 10 cash rows over 368 columns. The algorithm solves that smaller LP, and **postsolve** then maps its answer back to the original variables:

Performed postsolve
Solving the original LP from the solution after postsolve

In the second line HiGHS solves the original model starting from that mapped-back answer, to confirm it. Here that took no further pivots: the footer counts 14 iterations, the same 14 the iteration lines show.
The Iteration Lines Track the Objective and the Infeasibilities

Using EKK dual simplex solver - serial
  Iteration        Objective     Infeasibilities num(sum)
          0     0.0000000000e+00 Ph1: 0(0) <t>s
         14    -2.3489812061e+05 Pr: 0(0) <t>s
The first line names the algorithm: dual simplex (lesson 2.4.1), run on one thread ("serial"). EKK is the name of HiGHS's simplex code. Then one line every so often, with:

items: **Iteration**: pivots so far.

**Objective**: the objective at the current point. It is negative because HiGHS works on a minimization: maximizing $`\sum v_i f_i`$ is the same as minimizing $`-\sum v_i f_i`$, and the log shows the second. The sign flips back in the footer.

**Infeasibilities num(sum)**: how many quantities are still wrong, and by how much in total. `Pr:` counts **primal infeasibilities**, rows or bounds the current point breaks. `Du:` counts **dual infeasibilities**, variables whose reduced cost (lesson 2.3.3) says the objective could still improve. `Ph1:` marks phase 1, the start-up phase that looks for a first point to work from. A line can carry both counts, separated by `;`.

blocks.text: On a run of 14 pivots there are only two lines. On a long run there are many, and the pattern to look for is the counts falling to `0(0)` and the objective moving steadily. An objective that stalls for thousands of iterations while the counts stay put is what a struggling run looks like.
The Footer Is the Verdict: Status, Iterations, Objective

Model name          : funding-lp
Model status        : Optimal
Simplex   iterations: 14
Objective value     :  2.3489812061e+05
P-D objective error :  0.0000000000e+00
HiGHS run time      :          <t>
WARNING: Method setLogCallback is deprecated: alternative method is setCallback

items: **Model status** is the outcome. `Optimal` here.
**Simplex iterations** counts all pivots. A barrier run prints `IPM iterations` instead, IPM standing for **interior point method** (lesson 2.4.1); the word before `iterations` names the kind.
**Objective value** is in the model's own sense, so positive again: 234,898.12.

**P-D objective error** is the relative difference between the primal objective and the dual objective. At an optimum they are equal (strong duality, lesson 2.3.2), so 0 means the solver's two views of the answer agree.
**HiGHS run time** is the wall-clock time, masked here.
The **WARNING** comes from the way OR-Tools 9.15 attaches itself to HiGHS's log, and it is printed on every run, good or bad. It says nothing about your model.

blocks.text: The same facts are on the `SolveResult`, and a program reads them there rather than from the log:

print(f"termination: {result.termination.reason.name}")
print(f"simplex iterations: {result.solve_stats.simplex_iterations}")
print(f"objective: {result.objective_value():.4f}")

termination: OPTIMAL
simplex iterations: 14
objective: 234898.1206
The log is for people, and for what the result does not carry: the size before and after presolve, the coefficient ranges, the progress over time.
A Failed Run's Objective Line Means Nothing
Cut 2027's budget to $1,000k, below the $3,040k the must-do projects spend that year, and solve again:

must-do spend in 2027: 3,040; budget cut to 1,000
LP funding-lp has 49 rows; 410 cols; 706 nonzeros
Coefficient ranges:
  Matrix  [1e+00, 6e+03]
  Cost    [1e+01, 6e+03]
  Bound   [1e+00, 1e+00]
  RHS     [1e+00, 4e+04]
Presolving model
10 rows, 330 cols, 558 nonzeros  <t>s
Problem status detected on presolve: Infeasible
Model name          : funding-lp
Model status        : Infeasible
Objective value     :  0.0000000000e+00
HiGHS run time      :          <t>
WARNING: Method setLogCallback is deprecated: alternative method is setCallback
termination: INFEASIBLE; has a feasible solution: False

Presolve found the contradiction before any iteration, so there is no iteration line and no iteration count in the footer. Then the trap: the footer still prints `Objective value : 0.0`. There is no plan, so there is no objective; the line is printed anyway. A script that reads the objective line without the status line reports a plan worth $0.

The second run makes a common modelling slip: a new project's share is added to the objective with coefficient 900, but its upper bound of 1 and its spend in the cash rows are both forgotten. Nothing limits it:

Problem status detected on presolve: Primal infeasible or unbounded
Solving the original LP with primal simplex to determine infeasible or unbounded
Using EKK primal simplex solver
  Iteration        Objective     Infeasibilities num(sum)
          0    -6.1239605605e-04 Ph1: 39(6352); Du: 39(39) <t>s
         39     2.7463000000e+04 Pr: 0(0); Du: 362(2754.69) <t>s
Using EKK primal simplex solver
  Iteration        Objective     Infeasibilities num(sum)
         39     2.7462927508e+04 Pr: 0(0); Du: 362(299134) <t>s
         47     1.9614404655e+05 Pr: 0(0); Du: 184(48742.1) <t>s
Model name          : funding-lp
Model status        : Unbounded
Simplex   iterations: 47
Objective value     :  1.9614404655e+05
P-D objective error :               inf
HiGHS run time      :          <t>
WARNING: Method setLogCallback is deprecated: alternative method is setCallback
termination: UNBOUNDED; has a feasible solution: True

**Unbounded** means the objective can grow without limit while every row holds. Presolve could only tell that the model was infeasible *or* unbounded, so HiGHS ran primal simplex to decide which. Its lines show it: primal infeasibilities reach `0(0)` (it found points that keep every row), while dual infeasibilities never do (the objective can always still improve). The footer's objective, 196,144, is just where the solver stopped walking up an endless direction, and the P-D error is `inf` because there is no finite dual objective. The result even holds a feasible point, which is why the status, not the presence of a point or an objective, decides what a run means.
The rule for logs is the rule for results (lesson 1.1.3): read the status first. Only `Optimal` makes the objective line an answer.
<!-- practice 1 -->
GLOP and PDLP Logs Carry the Same Facts in Other Words
Every solver's log has a header, a presolve report, progress lines and a verdict, written in its own format. GLOP, on the same LP:

Initial problem: 49 rows, 410 columns, 706 entries with magnitude in [1.000000e+00, 5.990000e+03]
Objective stats: 400 non-zeros, range [1.200000e+01, 5.875000e+03]
Bounds stats: 488 non-zeros, range [1.000000e+00, 4.287000e+04]
Parameters: log_search_progress: true log_to_stdout: false
Starting presolve...
SingletonPreprocessor                        : 10(-39) rows, 409(-1) columns, 666(-40) entries. (<t>s)
FixedVariablePreprocessor                    : 10(-39) rows, 370(-40) columns, 603(-103) entries. (<t>s)
Reached fixed point after presolve pass #2
ProportionalColumnPreprocessor               : 10(-39) rows, 368(-42) columns, 601(-105) entries. (<t>s)
ScalingPreprocessor                          : 10(-39) rows, 368(-42) columns, 601(-105) entries. (<t>s)
Presolved problem: 10 rows, 368 columns, 601 entries with magnitude in [2.343434e-01, 1.000000e+00]

The same 49 rows, 410 columns and 706 entries, and the same reduction to 10 rows and 368 columns, now step by step: a row with a single variable (each must row) fixes that variable, the fixed variables leave, and columns that are multiples of one another are merged. Then **scaling**: GLOP multiplies rows and columns by factors so that the coefficients sit between 0.23 and 1, which keeps its tolerances meaningful. Scaling changes numbers, never the model's size: the row and column counts stay 10 and 368. GLOP's progress lines report the objective at some of its pivots, and its verdict is at the very end:

status: OPTIMAL
objective: 234898
iterations: 191
time: <t>
deterministic_time: 0.000442316
`deterministic_time` is a measure of work that, unlike `time`, is the same on every run of the same model and parameters, so it is the one to compare between runs.
PDLP's progress lines are a table, one row every 64 iterations here:

The first two columns count work. `iter#` is the iteration number. **`kkt_pass`** counts passes through the constraint matrix since the start: one pass is one product with the matrix and one with its transpose (for a quadratic objective, also one with its matrix), the work of one PDLP iteration (lesson 2.4.1). It is a decimal because a pass over part of the matrix counts as a fraction. Here it runs one ahead of the iteration count (65.0 at iteration 64, 257.0 at 256), and it is the fairer measure of PDLP's work between runs, since `time` depends on the machine.

The three columns after `time` are the three measures PDLP stops on (lesson 2.4.1), each relative to the size of the data: **rel_prim_res**, how much the rows are broken; **rel_dual_res**, how far the prices are from satisfying their own conditions; and **rel_gap**, the gap between the primal and dual objectives. The gap can be negative, so it is its size that has to be small. PDLP checks the three every so often (every 64 iterations in this run) and stops at the first check where all three are below its tolerance, here iteration 256. The middle block repeats the three in absolute terms: `prim_resid` is not zero at the end (0.0048 in the last table row), which is the sliver by which PDLP's point breaks rows and the reason its objective sat just above the simplex one in lesson 2.4.1.
After the verdict, PDLP's log ends with one more row in the same format as the table, under `Final solution stats`:

Termination reason: TERMINATION_REASON_OPTIMAL
Solution point type: POINT_TYPE_CURRENT_ITERATE
Final solution stats:
 iter# kkt_pass   time | rel_prim_res rel_dual_res      rel_gap |   prim_resid   dual_resid      obj_gap |     prim_obj     dual_obj |  prim_var_l2  dual_var_l2
   256    257.0    <t> |  1.57843e-07  3.71708e-09  2.67127e-08 |    0.0194902  9.25094e-05    0.0125496 |      234898.      234898. |      23088.4      3156.32

It repeats its own header, then gives the measures of the point PDLP actually returns. The line `Solution point type` names that point: the current iterate, the last $`(x, y)`$ pair. PDLP's log format documents that these final stats are measured on the original problem, whatever rescaling or presolve was used. The progress rows can describe a different candidate point (the format lists several, among them the average of the iterates since the last restart), which is why this row's measures differ from the table's row 256 although the iteration is the same. All three are still below $`10^{-6}`$. A program that parses the log meets this row like any progress row: it starts with an iteration number, and it is the last one.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **Ask for the log with `msg_cb`, and keep it as lines.** A list can be saved with the result and searched by a test.
**The header says what the solver received.** Check the sizes against the model; read the coefficient ranges for scaling trouble.
**Presolve shrinks the model before any iteration.** Fixed variables and redundant rows leave first; postsolve maps the answer back.
**The iteration lines track the objective and the infeasibilities.** `Pr:` counts broken rows, `Du:` counts possible improvements; both reach `0(0)` at an optimum.
**The footer is the verdict.** Status first; only `Optimal` makes the objective line an answer.
**GLOP and PDLP say the same things in other words.** PDLP stops when relative primal residual, dual residual and gap are all small.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: `LP <name> has R rows; C cols; N nonzeros`
smallest and largest absolute values of each kind
r rows left, k removed; c columns left, j removed
presolve settled the outcome; no iterations follow
phase 1 / primal / dual infeasibilities: count n, total s
an answer only when the status is Optimal
relative primal-dual objective difference; 0 at an optimum
the log, as a list of lines
whether the result holds an allowed point

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [MathOpt `solve.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/python/solve.py) (the `msg_cb` argument of `solve`, which hands back the underlying solver's log line by line); [Advanced LP Solving (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/lp/lp_advanced) (the tolerances behind "optimal", why badly scaled data defeats them, and why a solver's checks on the presolved model can disagree with the original, GLOP's `IMPRECISE`); [PDLP (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/lp/pdlp_math) (the rescaling PDLP applies and the residuals and gap its log reports); [PDLP `solve_log.proto`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/pdlp/solve_log.proto) (what a KKT matrix pass is, the point types, and the final solution stats measured on the original problem); [HiGHS, Solvers](https://ergo-code.github.io/HiGHS/dev/solvers/) (the dual simplex the log names as its default, and when interior point runs crossover).
Challenges

items: A colleague's HiGHS header says `Matrix [1e-03, 1e+08]`. Their costs are in dollars and their hours in minutes. What do you change, and what range would you expect after?
The funding LP's must rows were written as variable bounds instead, `add_variable(lb=1, ub=1)`. Predict the header's row count and the `Presolve reductions` line.
A nightly job greps the HiGHS log for `Objective value` and stores the number. Write the two lines of Python that make it safe.

blocks.text: Design Note: Keep the Log With the Result

A log printed to a terminal is gone when the job ends, and the week someone asks why a number moved is never the week the job ran. Saving the list `solve_with_log` returns next to the result costs a few kilobytes and answers the first three questions of any investigation: what model the solver received, what it removed, and how it ended.
